title: Confound Detective
summary: One fictional study with a confident causal claim, in two phases: sort four variables into confound, nuisance, part of the treatment and constant, then repair the design and watch the reported estimate walk toward a true effect the study cannot see. One repair removes no bias at all.
learningObjectives: State the two conditions a variable must meet to bias a comparison.
Distinguish a confound from a nuisance variable, and say what each does to an estimate.
Recognise that part of the manipulation is not a confound and cannot be controlled away.
Predict the effect of a design repair on the estimate rather than on the interval.
Explain why increasing the sample size does not reduce bias.
interactionTypes: four-way variable classification with explanatory feedback
live estimate recomputed as repairs are applied and undone
the true effect drawn on the same axis as the reported estimate
a repair that visibly removes no bias
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with each repair a full-width label containing a native checkbox so the whole row is the target and the tick is a non-colour state signal. The estimate figure prints the reported value and the true effect as text beside the marker and carries a description stating both and the gap between them. All three headline figures are text. No timed content and no motion.
dataStatus: Fictional. No real module, tutor, student, seminar or dataset is described, and the true effect is knowable only because the activity invented it.
simulationNotes: The estimate is the true effect of 3 marks plus the sum over open confounds of their bias times the fraction remaining. A repair removes a stated fraction of a named confound's bias and fractions combine multiplicatively across repairs. The bias figures are invented and were chosen to make the argument legible, not to estimate confounding in any real study: real confounds interact, point in opposite directions and sometimes cancel, and keeping them additive here is a deliberate simplification so the arithmetic can be followed. Sample size changes only the reported interval width, from plus or minus 5.1 at 60 students to plus or minus 2.0 at 400.
readmeTopic: confounding, and why bias and noise are different problems with different fixes
